extracted.intended_audience: ML/HCI researchers, ethics researchers, and practitioners designing dataset documentation, training, or studies of ethical sensitivity
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating studies and interventions (e.g., Datasheets, training, policies) to help ML engineers notice, particularize, and judge ethical issues in training data. Includes methodological guidance (think-aloud), curricular and organizational interventions, and measurement considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (noticing ethical issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologists must notice or recognize potential ethical problems in training data or tasks (the moment or events of 'recognition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition may not be a single 'moment of awakening' but an accumulation of concern; interventions like Datasheets or intermittent prompts can increase the frequency of recognition events; think-aloud can be used to measure recognition and identify cues, but recognition can be hard to observe precisely and time-to-first-recognition may be difficult to determine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularization (contextualizing and specifying ethical concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologists should particularize ethical problems by evaluating information sources, building familiarity with available options and resources, assessing risks, and understanding how problems and interventions fit the socio-technical context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularization skills can be taught (e.g., familiarity with common cues, historical examples, methods for evaluating risks). Think-aloud studies reveal how participants search for information, rely on examples, and reflect; measuring time spent on Datasheet sections could quantify how Datasheets support particularization. Note that particularization and judgment can loop back and forth; frequency and duration of these loops are meaningful data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment (formulating, deciding, and implementing responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologists should be able to formulate options, decide among trade-offs, and execute or implement chosen actions in response to identified ethical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rest’s verbs for judgment are 'formulating', 'deciding', and 'executing or implementing.' Think-aloud captures exploration, changing minds, trade-offs, and conditional reasoning (‘if [condition], then [judgment]...’). Ethnographic or longer-term studies may be needed to observe the execute/implement phase. Judgment frequently feeds back to particularization, so methods should allow observing those loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of context documents (Datasheets) as an intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Context documents such as Datasheets for Datasets should prompt recognition, support particularization, and guide judgment during dataset curation and model development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paper presents evidence that Datasheets can prompt recognition and support particularization; however, Datasheets may not be sufficient for ambiguous/less-discussed issues and filling them out may not be simple. Future work should test Datasheets with subtler ethical issues, measure how much time practitioners spend on sections, and develop best practices for writing thorough, effective Datasheets that account for affected communities and lived realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum design to foster ethical sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational curricula should be constructed to develop recognition, particularization, and judgment skills in ML learners and technologists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition can be taught by exposing learners to common cues, relevant ethical issues, and historical examples and by cultivating a habit of actively looking for problems. Particularization can be taught via evaluating information sources, methods for assessing risks, and developing a socio-technical perspective. Judgment can be practiced through case studies and exercises that expose learners to loops between particularization and judgment. Curricula should be adaptable to online courses, self-teaching, and on-the-job training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational policies, norms, and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should embed ethical sensitivity into norms, policies, job descriptions, and performance evaluations to make noticing and engaging with ethical issues part of workers’ responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions include intermittent prompts (to avoid habituation to regular forms), access to independent advice (legal counsel or third-party ethics review boards), and explicit incentives (positive feedback, raises, promotions) for ethical engagement. Such changes can reduce fear of retaliation and encourage reporting of concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think-aloud method appropriateness for studying ES
rubrics_metrics.description: Using think-aloud protocols is an effective method to observe ethical sensitivity—especially particularization and judgment—during simulated or situated work with data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think-aloud lets researchers watch participants search for information, use examples, reflect, explore options, and change judgments—capturing richer, process-oriented data than surveys focused on decisions alone. It can reveal how context affects particularization and the dynamics of judgment. However, think-aloud has difficulties (e.g., might not capture execute/implement phase, potential reactivity) and should be chosen with awareness of trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design: participant familiarity and sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must manage variation in participants’ familiarity with data types, domains, regulatory environments, and ML techniques, and consider how expertise mediates ethical sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include randomization across familiarity levels or targeted recruitment of domain-expert participants to study domain-specific problems. Balance experience across study groups if experience is an explanatory variable; small samples and uneven randomization limit interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design: salience/obviousness of embedded cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must decide how obvious ethical problems or cues embedded in tasks should be, as cue salience affects what aspect of ethical sensitivity is observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot testing can assess cue salience. Manipulating obviousness allows focusing on different phenomena: subtle cues with many participants for nuanced recognition data, or highly salient issues to gather later-stage particularization and judgment data. News attention or regulatory changes can alter salience during a study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design: task duration and ecological validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about how long participants work on tasks and the environment (lab vs real work) affect which features of ethical sensitivity are observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sessions (e.g., 30 minutes) can yield rich initial data; longer-term projects reveal feedback between particularization and judgment, changes from new information/testing, and how design commitments alter risk assessments. Lab/provided-computer setups give more control and granular behavioral data (e.g., keystrokes, eye-tracking) but may reduce ecological validity; observing participants in their real environment preserves natural work practices but may limit granular measurement and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and data collection: capture positionality and demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting participant positionality (race, gender, sexuality, country of origin, job role, years of experience) is important because awareness, beliefs, and standpoint likely influence particularization and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not collecting such data limits contextual interpretation of findings; future studies should include these variables and consider how they mediate ethical sensitivity to appropriately target interventions in training, team composition, and task design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement challenges: defining and detecting recognition events and loops
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalizing and detecting recognition events and the loops between particularization and judgment is methodologically challenging but revealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers can measure the quantity of recognition events, identify triggers and cues, and observe interruptions of judgment to return to particularization. Questions to investigate include whether fewer loops indicate confidence or complacency, whether frequent/longer pauses are desirable in complex work, and what characterizes useful versus delaying loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative testing of ethics interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasheets should be tested alongside other context documents and interventions (e.g., Algorithmic Impact Assessments, envisioning cards, adversary cards, design workbooks) to understand relative effectiveness and how each elicits or changes ethical sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future work should compare interventions across contexts and with subtler ethical problems and should develop metrics to evaluate how interventions change recognition, particularization, and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and transparency in reporting study constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should explicitly report study limitations (e.g., sample size, non-collection of demographics, timing coinciding with news events) that affect generalizability and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, this study’s ethical issue was highly publicized during data collection which likely increased recognition; small sample sizes and missing demographic variables limit claims. Transparency about such constraints helps contextualize findings and guide future replication or extension studies.
